question: Using the customary setting of the mathematics used for quantum mechanics, is it possible to prove the existence of Gödelßs god-like entities?

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, not as a theorem of the mathematics that is actually used in quantum theory.

The customary mathematics of non-relativistic quantum mechanics is ordinary classical mathematics: ZFC set theory plus analysis, linear algebra over C, separable complex Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, spectral theory, etc. That is a first order formal system, and it is perfectly able to encode syntax and formalize modal logic S5 in the usual way. In that sense Gödel’s ontological argument can be written down in the language of the mathematics of QM and it is a perfectly correct derivation in S5 from its premises

P1  ∀P [Pos(P) → □Pos(P)]
P2  Pos(P) → Pos(¬P is non-positive)
...
etc.

The conclusion G  ∃x □∀P [Pos(P)→P(x)] is a theorem of S5 + those axioms. So the argument is formalizable inside the same metamathematics that underlies Hilbert-space theory.

What the formalization does not give you is a mathematical theorem of the physics. The predicate Pos, “is a positive property”, the modal operators □, ◇ read as metaphysical necessity/possibility, and the axiom that the property “being an ens realissimum” is positive, are not definitions in set theory, functional analysis or quantum mechanics. They are philosophical premises. The mathematics of QM provides no meaning for Pos and no axioms that make Pos(P) true of the property “being omnipotent”, “being omniscient”, etc., and it gives no bridge from the formal existence of a maximally great object in a Kripke model of S5 to the existence of a physical or ontological entity in the world.

Hence at best you get a conditional consistency statement: if the Gödel-Plantinga axioms about positive properties are consistent with ZFC, then ZFC proves the consistency of the S5 theory with a God-like witness. It is not a proof of the physical existence of a Gödelian God-like entity from the Hilbert space formalism alone, and the existence claim remains extramathematical. In the strict mathematical sense the argument adds nothing to the mathematics actually used for quantum mechanics.

2.text:
In the ordinary mathematics that is used to formulate quantum mechanics the
proof is available.

The mathematics that is actually used in textbook quantum mechanics is
essentially ZFC set theory plus normed linear algebra over C.  In
particular it is classical mathematics with the ordinary Boolean
propositional and first order predicate calculus as meta logic and with
classical S5 modal logic available as a conservative extension of
it.  Gödel’s ontological argument can be written as an ordinary
first order S5 theory in the language

* $P x$ : $x$ has the property $P$,
* $P$ is positive,
* $G(x)\equiv \forall P\,[\,{\rm Positive}(P)\to P x\,]$,
* $\Box$, $\Diamond$, $\to$, $\wedge$, $\vee$, $\neg$, $\forall$, $\exists$,

with the usual Gödel axioms for positivity and for the modal
principle

* $\Box\,\forall P\,[\,{\rm Positive}(P)\to \Box\,{\rm Positive}(P)\,]$,
* $\Box\,\forall P\,[\,{\rm Positive}(P)\to {\rm Positive}(\Box P)\,]$,
* $\Box\,\forall P\,[\,{\rm Positive}(P)\to {\rm Positive}(\neg P)\to
 {\rm Positive}(\neg P)\,]$ etc.,

and the essentially classical definition

* $\Box\exists x\,G(x)\to \exists x\,G(x)$.

On these axioms Gödel derives in S5

* $\Box\exists x\,G(x)$,
* $\exists x\,G(x)$,

i.e. the existence of a being which has all positive properties, in
particular a necessarily existent maximally great being.  The derivation
is a purely syntactic derivation in classical modal logic.  Classical
modal logic is a fragment of the set theory/functional analysis that
underlies the Hilbert space formalism of quantum mechanics, so the
derivation can be carried out inside the ordinary mathematics of
quantum theory.  In that formal sense a god-like, maximally positive,
necessarily existent entity exists in every model of the Gödel axioms.

That is all that is obtained.  The theorem is conditional on the
intensional notion of `positive property' and on the S5 modal
principles.  It is a consistency/formal existence result, not an
empirical demonstration of a physical entity, and quantum mechanics adds
no new physical content to it.  In particular if the logic is taken
strictly to be the lattice logic of closed subspaces of a Hilbert space,
the orthomodular quantum logic, the distributive laws and the classical
modal inferences on which Gödel’s derivation rests are not valid, so
the argument does not survive a strictly quantum-logical reading.  In
the physical sense there is no proof of the existence of a Gödel
god-like entity from quantum mechanics.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. In the customary mathematical setting that is actually used in working quantum mechanics you are working inside ordinary classical mathematics — separable complex Hilbert spaces, bounded operators, the spectral theorem, etc. — all formalised in ZF set theory with first-order classical logic. Gödel’s ontological argument is not a first-order arithmetical statement. It is a second-order modal argument whose positive property axioms and the S5 necessity operator have to be interpreted over a complete Boolean algebra of properties.

The standard quantum formalism does not give you that Boolean algebra. The lattice of physical propositions is the lattice of projection operators on a Hilbert space, which is orthomodular and in general non-distributive. In particular the usual modal accessibility relation required for a normal Kripke frame for S5 is a classical binary relation on a set of possible worlds with classical truth values. That structure is not present in the C*-algebraic / Hilbert-space mathematics that physicists actually use, and importing it would be exactly an extension of the customary mathematics, not an internal result of it.

Hence within the usual quantum-mechanical mathematics — linear algebra over ℂ, functional analysis and classical first-order set theory — the second-order modal language in which Gödel’s axioms are expressed cannot even be interpreted without a non-trivial metamathematical expansion, and the proof of existence of a God-like entity does not go through on the internal resources of the theory.

6.text:
The formalism of non-relativistic quantum mechanics is set theory plus analysis
in its ordinary classical form. A quantum theory is a separable complex
Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, a self-adjoint operator algebra $\mathcal A(\mathcal
H)$, states as normalised vectors or density operators on $\mathcal H$ and the
usual Borel functional calculus. That is ZFC + classical analysis with
classical first-order logic. No new ontological principle is added by the
Hilbert space structure.

Gödel's ontological argument is a theorem of a modal theory of properties.
Let $P$ be the predicate “is positive’’ and let 
$G x\equiv \forall P\,[P(x)\rightarrow P(x)]$ etc. be the usual Gödel
definitions of essentially positive and god-like. With the axioms

* $P$ is consistent,
* positive properties are closed under entailment and under conj.
* $\Box\forall x\,[\,\Phi(x)\rightarrow \exists y\,\Phi(y)\,]$
* $\forall x\,[\,G x\rightarrow P x\,]$,
* $\forall x\,[\,G x\rightarrow \Box\exists y\,G y\,]$,

and the modal logic S5, one gets $\exists x\,G x$, i.e. necessarily
$\exists x\,G x$. The proof is purely logical, it refers to an abstract
universe of properties and to the modal operators $\square,\Diamond$.
It uses no structure of $\mathcal H$, no spectral measure, no commutation
relations, no $\mathbf C$-linearity, and no empirical postulate of quantum
theory at all.

Hence the mathematics used for quantum mechanics supplies no new axioms
about positivity, essence or necessity, and it supplies no physical
interpretation of the predicate $P$ which would make the Gödel axioms true
of physical states, observables or Hilbert-space vectors. In particular the
theory of quantum mechanics is formulated in classical logic, and Gödel's
proof is normally stated in classical first order logic plus S5. You can of
course write the modal theory down in the same metamathematical background
in which QM is written, i.e. you can formalise it in ZFC, so the proof is
formally embeddable in the same background mathematics. That embedding
adds nothing physical and does not turn the metaphysical claim
$\exists x\,G x$ into a consequence of the postulates of quantum theory.
In a physically meaningful sense the existence of a Gödel god-like being is
therefore not a consequence of, and is not provable from, the Hilbert-space
formalism of quantum mechanics.  The argument remains a formal modal-logical
claim whose truth is independent of the structure of $\mathcal H$.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The customary mathematical setting that underlies textbook quantum mechanics is ordinary classical mathematics — ZF set theory in first-order logic with Hilbert spaces over C, bounded operators, spectral theory, etc. Gödel’s ontological argument is a modal argument: its key axioms, in particular □P → P and the modal closure conditions, are not statements in first-order arithmetic/set theory at all, but assertions in a quantified modal language with an S5 necessity operator. 

Kripke semantics for S5 is a meta-logical device for interpreting that modal language; it is not a structure that lives inside the Hilbert space formalism of quantum mechanics. There is no canonical interpretation of the modal operator □ as a self-adjoint operator, a projector, or any other object of the C*-algebraic / functional analytic framework actually used in QM, and the possible-worlds accessibility relation of S5 has no natural counterpart in the standard model-theoretic semantics for Hilbert spaces. In other words one can of course formalise Gödel’s axioms in S5 and verify them in a Kripke model at the meta-level, but that verification does not take place within, nor is it expressible in, the customary first-order mathematics of quantum mechanics. Without internalising the modal apparatus the ontological conclusion is not a theorem of the mathematical theory actually used for QM.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Formally you can reproduce Gödel’s modal ontological argument in the
formal system that is the usual background of quantum theory, but you do not
thereby get an unconditional mathematical / physical existence proof of a
God-like being.

The mathematics customarily used for quantum mechanics is ordinary
classical mathematics: ZFC set theory plus analysis and the theory of
complex Hilbert spaces, i.e. a recursively axiomatizable extension of
Peano arithmetic. First order modal logic S5 and the first order language
in which Gödel formalises “positive property”, “essence”, “necessary
existence”, etc. can be coded in that system. On that coding Gödel’s
argument is a perfectly ordinary derivation:

If P is positive then □P, 
If P is positive then ¬P is not positive, 
etc. 
Necessary existence is positive, 
hence a being possessing all positive properties exists in the sense of
S5.

So the derivation is formally possible and is in fact valid in the
usual formalisation. It is however a conditional derivation. The theorem
is

Axioms about positivity + S5 modality → □∃x Gx

and not a theorem of ZFC+analysis alone. The notion of a “positive
property’’ and the axioms

* P positive → □P positive
* Possibly P → P implies P positive → □P
* etc.

are essentially metaphysical stipulations about value-laden concepts.
They are not part of the mathematics of Hilbert spaces, operators,
spectra etc. that is used in quantum mechanics, and they are not
decidable or empirically testable within that mathematics. In particular
the proof does not give a construction, a model, or a measurable
property in a Hilbert space; it gives a modal consequence of a set of
philosophical premises.

In the scientific sense therefore the mathematics of quantum mechanics
does not prove the existence of a Gödelian God-like entity. It can only
host the formal encoding of Gödel’s ontological argument, whose
conclusion is as strong as, and no stronger than, the controversial
axioms about positivity and necessary existence on which it is based.
That is the usual way in which the argument is understood: valid modulo
its premises, not a mathematical existence theorem in the sense used in
physics.

11.text:
In the physics sense no. 

The mathematics that is actually used to do quantum mechanics is
the ordinary set-theoretic first order mathematics of complex
Hilbert spaces, $C^{*}$-algebras, spectral theory etc., i.e. first
order ZFC + analysis.  In that language you have vectors, operators,
spectra, probabilities and the usual classical Boolean propositional
logic which is used externally to state theorems about the formalism.

Godel’s ontological argument is a derivation in a quantified modal
logic, usually S5, from a set of metaphysical premises about
positivity of properties,

* $P(x)\to \neg P(\neg x)$,
* $\exists x\,P(x)$ is positive,
* necessary existence is positive,
* etc.,

and the modal axiom $ \Box A\to A$ and the S5 accessibility
relation.  The derivation

$ \vdash_{S5} \Box \exists x\,G(x) $

for $G(x)$ the God-like predicate “has all positive properties” is
a perfectly good formal derivation once the positivity axioms and the
modal logic are admitted. It is therefore a theorem of the
underlying set-theoretic language in the same sense that any theorem
of modal logic is. In that purely formal sense the argument can be
written down in the first order language that underlies the
Hilbert-space formalism.

It is not a theorem of functional analysis, of quantum theory, or of
any empirically grounded part of the physics formalism. The
positivity axioms, the notion of a “positive property”, the modal
operator $\Box$, and the identification of necessary existence with
the property possessed by a maximally great being, are extra-
mathematical, metaphysical premises. They have no translation into
observables, states, Hamiltonians or transition amplitudes and they
are not derivable from the postulates of quantum mechanics. Hence
quantum mechanics, taken as a physical theory, gives no empirical
justification for the premises and consequently gives no physical
proof of the existence of a Godel god-like entity. The derivation is
conditional on accepting the metaphysical axioms; without them the
formalism of QM is silent on the question.

3.text:
In the ordinary mathematical foundations of non-relativistic quantum
mechanics you are working up to isomorphism with

* ZFC + the usual real and complex analysis,
* a separable complex Hilbert space ${\cal H}$, the lattice
${\cal P}({\cal H})$ of orthogonal projections, self adjoint operators,
etc.

i.e. with ordinary mathematics.  What is usually called the Hilbert
space formalism is classical first order mathematics.  Quantum logic in
the strictly physical sense is the orthomodular lattice ${\cal P}({\cal
H})$ and it is a non-distributive, non Boolean logic.  The Gödel
ontological argument is a theorem of modal propositional logic $S5$
with a primitive predicate $P x$ for ``$x$ is a positive property'' and
the two modal axioms

* $\Box \forall x\,(P x\to Px)$,
* $\forall x\,\Box(Px\to \Diamond Ex)$,

together with the usual axioms of the notion of perfection, e.g.

* $\forall x\,\Box(Px\to\neg P\neg x)$,
* $\forall x\,\Box(Px\to P\Box Px)$,

and the definition $G x\equiv \forall P\,(Px\to xP)$ of a God-like
being.  Under those axioms $S5$ does indeed prove

$$\Box \exists x\,Gx \qquad{\rm and}\qquad \exists x\,Gx ,$$

and the proof can be carried out in any classical first order
background theory strong enough to interpret $S5$, in particular in
ZFC.

That is all that is ever meant by “formalising” Gödel’s argument in
the mathematics that underlies quantum theory.  No theorem about
Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, spectra, projection valued
measures etc. is thereby obtained. The “positive property’’ predicate
$P$, the modal operators $\Box,\Diamond$, and the essentially perfect
being $G$ have no canonical interpretation as closed subspaces,
projections or self-adjoint operators on ${\cal H}$.  In particular the
distributive Boolean connectives and the S5 Kripke semantics on which
the derivation rests are not the orthomodular logic of ${\cal P}({\cal
H})$.  In the quantum logical setting the law of distributivity which
is used essentially in the modal derivation fails, and the usual S5
modal closure properties have no natural realisation in the lattice of
quantum propositions.

Hence the existence of a Gödelian essentially perfect being is not a
theorem of the Hilbert-space theory of quantum mechanics.  Formally
you can write the modal proof down in the set-theoretic language in
which ${\cal H}$ is defined, but the proof is conditional on the
philosophical axioms about positivity and on the classical modal
logic S5.  Those axioms are extra-mathematical; they are not theorems
of, nor are they definable in, the customary Hilbert-space
mathematics of quantum mechanics, and in the genuine quantum logical
logic of the theory the argument does not go through.  The existence
claim remains a conditional modal-logical consequence of unproved
metaphysical premises, not a mathematical theorem about quantum
mechanics.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The mathematics that is actually in routine use for non-relativistic quantum mechanics is essentially classical analysis on complex separable Hilbert spaces — a development within ZFC with ordinary first-order classical logic and the usual real/complex arithmetic. 

Gödel’s ontological argument is a modal argument about properties and essence. Even when it is formalised in propositional modal logic S5, its rendering inside the Hilbert-space formalism would require an internal interpretation of the modal operators □ and ◇ as operators on states or observables, and an internal quantification over the full property space of a being. 

In the customary setting the only objects available are vectors, operators, spectra and the usual set-theoretic functions that build them. There is no canonical Kripke frame of possible worlds internal to that structure, and no way within the ordinary Hilbert-space / C*-algebra calculus to express the modal axioms — in particular the Barcan formula and the S5 accessibility relation — without stepping outside the first-order analytic language in which quantum mechanics is formulated. In other words, the modal quantifiers needed for the Anselmian perfection concept are not definable as self-adjoint operators or as elements of a Hilbert space, so the ontological proof cannot be carried out as a theorem of the mathematics one actually uses for quantum mechanics. At best one can import a separate modal metalogic, which is an extension of, not part of, the customary quantum-mechanical framework.

8.text:
In the physics the formalism is used for predictions, not for metaphysics.
The mathematical language that is normally used for non-relativistic
quantum mechanics is the classical metatheory of complex separable
Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, spectral measures etc.  In the
metatheory the reasoning is ordinary classical first/second order logic
and in particular it is Boolean and distributive.  Gödel's ontological
argument can be formalised in that metatheory and in the modal logic S5
with the usual positivity axioms

* P is positive -> necessarily P is positive,
* necessarily P -> P is possibly P,

etc., it is a theorem that a God-like being, i.e. a being that has every
positive property and in particular the property of necessary existence,
exists.  That is a theorem of the classical modal logic that you can
write down in ZFC, the set theory in which Hilbert space theory is set
up.

It is not a theorem of the native propositional calculus of quantum
mechanics.  The physical propositions of a quantum system are the lattice
L(H) of closed subspaces, or orthoprojectors, of the Hilbert space H.
L(H) is orthomodular, not Boolean, and in particular not distributive.
The logic that is intrinsic to the formalism is quantum logic.  Classical
modal S5, and the distributive Boolean algebra of properties on which
Gödel's definition of positivity, closure under implication and the
axiom Necessarily Positive are formulated, are not realised as an
intrinsic part of L(H).  In particular the Kochen–Specker type
non-contextuality of L(H) means that there is no global two-valued
valuation that makes all positive properties simultaneously definite,
whereas a Gödel god is precisely the maximal element that possesses
every positive property at once and necessarily so.

Hence no existence theorem for a Gödel god-like entity is derivable from
the Hilbert-space formalism itself.  One can of course import the
classical S5 ontological argument into the classical metatheory in which
the mathematics of quantum mechanics is written, and in that external
metatheory the Gödel proof goes through conditionally on its modal
positivity axioms.  That is a formalisation of a philosophical argument,
not a physical consequence of the quantum mechanical formalism.  Within
the native quantum logical structure the distributive and modal
infrastructure required by Gödel's proof is absent and the proof breaks
down.

10.text:
In the thin formal sense the proof can be written down, in the thick
ontological sense it can not.

The ordinary mathematical infrastructure of non-relativistic quantum
mechanics is ZFC + ordinary analysis, i.e. the theory of complex
separable Hilbert spaces, bounded and unbounded self-adjoint operators,
spectral measures etc.  First order modal logic S5 and the five
axioms of positivity that Gödel uses for $G:=$ “a being than which no
greater can be conceived’’ are arithmetical in nature and are
formalizable in the background set theory that underlies functional
analysis.  Once the modal operators $\Box ,\Diamond$ are coded in the
usual Kripke semantics, the S5 derivation

* $P(x)\to \Box P(x)$ for $P$ positive,
* $\Box\, \exists x\,A(x)\to\exists x\,\Box A(x)$,
* $\exists x\,\Box\,\Phi(x)\to\Diamond\,\exists x\,\Phi(x)$,

etc., and in particular Gödel’s

$G\to\Box G,\qquad \Diamond \exists x\,x\;{\rm is\;God-like}\to
\exists x\,\Box x\;{\rm is\;God-like},$

goes through in the same first-order set theory that proves the
existence of $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3})$, the spectral theorem and the
usual postulates of QM.  So the syntactic derivation can be reproduced
verbatim in the language of the mathematics used for QM.

What is not produced is a physical or “real’’ existence proof.  The
derivation is a derivation of $\Box\exists!x\,G(x)$ from the purely
philosophical axioms of positivity, necessity of the positive and the
S5 modal frame.  The Hilbert-space formalism gives no semantics for
the modal operators “necessarily”, “positive property”, “greater than”,
nor does it supply any empirical content to the notion of a
maximally great being.  In particular the proof is a proof of
consistency and derivability in a formal system, not a theorem about
self-adjoint operators, spectra or measurement outcomes.

If the non-classical propositional calculus associated with quantum
mechanics, the orthomodular lattice of projections, is taken as the
logic of physical propositions, the distributive law on which the
ordinary S5 derivation rests fails in quantum logic and the Gödel
derivation does not even go through syntactically.  In the material
sense there is therefore no new ontological warrant for God’s
existence coming from the customary mathematics of quantum mechanics.
The mathematics can at best host the formal modal argument; it does
not prove the existence of a god-like entity in the world.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. In the customary mathematical setting that is actually used for quantum mechanics – essentially ZF set theory together with the analytic machinery of complex separable Hilbert spaces, bounded self-adjoint operators, C*-algebras and the usual classical first-order logic in which physical propositions are formulated – there is no internal place for Gödel’s modal apparatus.

Gödel’s ontological argument is formulated in a second-order modal language with an S5 necessity operator and a comprehension schema for properties. Its validity is normally exhibited in a meta-logical Kripke semantics for S5. That semantics lives in the logic of possible worlds, not in the Hilbert-space formalism itself. The Hilbert-space formalism of QM provides a model for the quantum state space, observables and probabilities, but it does not furnish an interpretation of the modal operator □, nor does it provide a domain of “positive” properties with the necessary closure conditions required for Gödel’s axioms P1–P4 and the essence axiom.

In other words one can embed the syntax of Gödel’s proof in ZF, and one can prove its validity with respect to a Kripke model in the meta-theory, but the proof cannot be carried out as an internal theorem of the mathematical structures that do the physical work in quantum mechanics. The physical mathematics is essentially non-modal linear algebra over ℂ; once you stay strictly inside that customary setting the modal-combinatorial resources needed for the God-like essence argument are simply absent, so no existence theorem for Gödel’s god-like entities is derivable there.

relations, no $\mathbf C$-linearity, and no empirical postulate of quantum
theory at all.

Hence the mathematics used for quantum mechanics supplies no new axioms
about positivity, essence or necessity, and it supplies no physical
interpretation of the predicate $P$ which would make the Gödel axioms true
of physical states, observables or Hilbert-space vectors. In particular the
theory of quantum mechanics is formulated in classical logic, and Gödel's
proof is normally stated in classical first order logic plus S5. You can of
course write the modal theory down in the same metamathematical background
in which QM is written, i.e. you can formalise it in ZFC, so the proof is
formally embeddable in the same background mathematics. That embedding
adds nothing physical and does not turn the metaphysical claim
$\exists x\,G x$ into a consequence of the postulates of quantum theory.
In a physically meaningful sense the existence of a Gödel god-like being is
therefore not a consequence of, and is not provable from, the Hilbert-space
formalism of quantum mechanics.  The argument remains a formal modal-logical
claim whose truth is independent of the structure of $\mathcal H$.

In other words one can of course formalise Gödel’s axioms in S5 and verify them in a Kripke model at the meta-level, but that verification does not take place within, nor is it expressible in, the customary first-order mathematics of quantum mechanics. Formally you can reproduce Gödel’s modal ontological argument in the
formal system that is the usual background of quantum theory, but you do not
thereby get an unconditional mathematical / physical existence proof of a
God-like being.

The mathematics customarily used for quantum mechanics is ordinary
classical mathematics: ZFC set theory plus analysis and the theory of
complex Hilbert spaces, i.e. a recursively axiomatizable extension of
Peano arithmetic. First order modal logic S5 and the first order language
in which Gödel formalises “positive property”, “essence”, “necessary
existence”, etc. can be coded in that system. On that coding Gödel’s
argument is a perfectly ordinary derivation:

If P is positive then □P, 
If P is positive then ¬P is not positive, 
etc. 
Necessary existence is positive, 
hence a being possessing all positive properties exists in the sense of
S5.

So the derivation is formally possible and is in fact valid in the
usual formalisation. It is however a conditional derivation. The theorem
is

Axioms about positivity + S5 modality → □∃x Gx

and not a theorem of ZFC+analysis alone. The notion of a “positive
property’’ and the axioms

* P positive → □P positive
* Possibly P → P implies P positive → □P
* etc.

are essentially metaphysical stipulations about value-laden concepts.
They are not part of the mathematics of Hilbert spaces, operators,
spectra etc. that is used in quantum mechanics, and they are not
decidable or empirically testable within that mathematics. In particular
the proof does not give a construction, a model, or a measurable
property in a Hilbert space; it gives a modal consequence of a set of
philosophical premises.

In the scientific sense therefore the mathematics of quantum mechanics
does not prove the existence of a Gödelian God-like entity. It can only
host the formal encoding of Gödel’s ontological argument, whose
conclusion is as strong as, and no stronger than, the controversial
axioms about positivity and necessary existence on which it is based.
That is the usual way in which the argument is understood: valid modulo
its premises, not a mathematical existence theorem in the sense used in
physics.

In the physics sense no. 

The mathematics that is actually used to do quantum mechanics is
the ordinary set-theoretic first order mathematics of complex
Hilbert spaces, $C^{*}$-algebras, spectral theory etc., i.e. first
order ZFC + analysis.  In that language you have vectors, operators,
spectra, probabilities and the usual classical Boolean propositional
logic which is used externally to state theorems about the formalism.

Godel’s ontological argument is a derivation in a quantified modal
logic, usually S5, from a set of metaphysical premises about
positivity of properties,

* $P(x)\to \neg P(\neg x)$,
* $\exists x\,P(x)$ is positive,
* necessary existence is positive,
* etc.,

and the modal axiom $ \Box A\to A$ and the S5 accessibility
relation.  The derivation

$ \vdash_{S5} \Box \exists x\,G(x) $

for $G(x)$ the God-like predicate “has all positive properties” is
a perfectly good formal derivation once the positivity axioms and the
modal logic are admitted. It is therefore a theorem of the
underlying set-theoretic language in the same sense that any theorem
of modal logic is. In that purely formal sense the argument can be
written down in the first order language that underlies the
Hilbert-space formalism.

It is not a theorem of functional analysis, of quantum theory, or of
any empirically grounded part of the physics formalism. The
positivity axioms, the notion of a “positive property”, the modal
operator $\Box$, and the identification of necessary existence with
the property possessed by a maximally great being, are extra-
mathematical, metaphysical premises. They have no translation into
observables, states, Hamiltonians or transition amplitudes and they
are not derivable from the postulates of quantum mechanics. Hence
quantum mechanics, taken as a physical theory, gives no empirical
justification for the premises and consequently gives no physical
proof of the existence of a Godel god-like entity. The derivation is
conditional on accepting the metaphysical axioms; without them the
formalism of QM is silent on the question.
public_text.3:
In the ordinary mathematical foundations of non-relativistic quantum
mechanics you are working up to isomorphism with

* ZFC + the usual real and complex analysis,
* a separable complex Hilbert space ${\cal H}$, the lattice
${\cal P}({\cal H})$ of orthogonal projections, self adjoint operators,
etc.

i.e. with ordinary mathematics.  What is usually called the Hilbert
space formalism is classical first order mathematics.  Quantum logic in
the strictly physical sense is the orthomodular lattice ${\cal P}({\cal
H})$ and it is a non-distributive, non Boolean logic.  The Gödel
ontological argument is a theorem of modal propositional logic $S5$
with a primitive predicate $P x$ for ``$x$ is a positive property'' and
the two modal axioms

* $\Box \forall x\,(P x\to Px)$,
* $\forall x\,\Box(Px\to \Diamond Ex)$,

together with the usual axioms of the notion of perfection, e.g.

* $\forall x\,\Box(Px\to\neg P\neg x)$,
* $\forall x\,\Box(Px\to P\Box Px)$,

and the definition $G x\equiv \forall P\,(Px\to xP)$ of a God-like
being.  Under those axioms $S5$ does indeed prove

$$\Box \exists x\,Gx \qquad{\rm and}\qquad \exists x\,Gx ,$$

and the proof can be carried out in any classical first order
background theory strong enough to interpret $S5$, in particular in
ZFC.

That is all that is ever meant by “formalising” Gödel’s argument in
the mathematics that underlies quantum theory.  No theorem about
Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, spectra, projection valued
measures etc. is thereby obtained. The “positive property’’ predicate
$P$, the modal operators $\Box,\Diamond$, and the essentially perfect
being $G$ have no canonical interpretation as closed subspaces,
projections or self-adjoint operators on ${\cal H}$.  In particular the
distributive Boolean connectives and the S5 Kripke semantics on which
the derivation rests are not the orthomodular logic of ${\cal P}({\cal
H})$.  In the quantum logical setting the law of distributivity which
is used essentially in the modal derivation fails, and the usual S5
modal closure properties have no natural realisation in the lattice of
quantum propositions.

Hence the existence of a Gödelian essentially perfect being is not a
theorem of the Hilbert-space theory of quantum mechanics.  Formally
you can write the modal proof down in the set-theoretic language in
which ${\cal H}$ is defined, but the proof is conditional on the
philosophical axioms about positivity and on the classical modal
logic S5.  Those axioms are extra-mathematical; they are not theorems
of, nor are they definable in, the customary Hilbert-space
mathematics of quantum mechanics, and in the genuine quantum logical
logic of the theory the argument does not go through.  The existence
claim remains a conditional modal-logical consequence of unproved
metaphysical premises, not a mathematical theorem about quantum
mechanics.

Even when it is formalised in propositional modal logic S5, its rendering inside the Hilbert-space formalism would require an internal interpretation of the modal operators □ and ◇ as operators on states or observables, and an internal quantification over the full property space of a being.

There is no canonical Kripke frame of possible worlds internal to that structure, and no way within the ordinary Hilbert-space / C*-algebra calculus to express the modal axioms — in particular the Barcan formula and the S5 accessibility relation — without stepping outside the first-order analytic language in which quantum mechanics is formulated. In other words, the modal quantifiers needed for the Anselmian perfection concept are not definable as self-adjoint operators or as elements of a Hilbert space, so the ontological proof cannot be carried out as a theorem of the mathematics one actually uses for quantum mechanics. In the physics the formalism is used for predictions, not for metaphysics.
The mathematical language that is normally used for non-relativistic
quantum mechanics is the classical metatheory of complex separable
Hilbert spaces, self-adjoint operators, spectral measures etc.  In the
metatheory the reasoning is ordinary classical first/second order logic
and in particular it is Boolean and distributive.  Gödel's ontological
argument can be formalised in that metatheory and in the modal logic S5
with the usual positivity axioms

* P is positive -> necessarily P is positive,
* necessarily P -> P is possibly P,

etc., it is a theorem that a God-like being, i.e. a being that has every
positive property and in particular the property of necessary existence,
exists.  That is a theorem of the classical modal logic that you can
write down in ZFC, the set theory in which Hilbert space theory is set
up.

It is not a theorem of the native propositional calculus of quantum
mechanics.  The physical propositions of a quantum system are the lattice
L(H) of closed subspaces, or orthoprojectors, of the Hilbert space H.
L(H) is orthomodular, not Boolean, and in particular not distributive.
The logic that is intrinsic to the formalism is quantum logic.  Classical
modal S5, and the distributive Boolean algebra of properties on which
Gödel's definition of positivity, closure under implication and the
axiom Necessarily Positive are formulated, are not realised as an
intrinsic part of L(H).  In particular the Kochen–Specker type
non-contextuality of L(H) means that there is no global two-valued
valuation that makes all positive properties simultaneously definite,
whereas a Gödel god is precisely the maximal element that possesses
every positive property at once and necessarily so.

Hence no existence theorem for a Gödel god-like entity is derivable from
the Hilbert-space formalism itself.  One can of course import the
classical S5 ontological argument into the classical metatheory in which
the mathematics of quantum mechanics is written, and in that external
metatheory the Gödel proof goes through conditionally on its modal
positivity axioms.  That is a formalisation of a philosophical argument,
not a physical consequence of the quantum mechanical formalism.  Within
the native quantum logical structure the distributive and modal
infrastructure required by Gödel's proof is absent and the proof breaks
down.

In the thin formal sense the proof can be written down, in the thick
ontological sense it can not.

The ordinary mathematical infrastructure of non-relativistic quantum
mechanics is ZFC + ordinary analysis, i.e. the theory of complex
separable Hilbert spaces, bounded and unbounded self-adjoint operators,
spectral measures etc.  First order modal logic S5 and the five
axioms of positivity that Gödel uses for $G:=$ “a being than which no
greater can be conceived’’ are arithmetical in nature and are
formalizable in the background set theory that underlies functional
analysis.  Once the modal operators $\Box ,\Diamond$ are coded in the
usual Kripke semantics, the S5 derivation

* $P(x)\to \Box P(x)$ for $P$ positive,
* $\Box\, \exists x\,A(x)\to\exists x\,\Box A(x)$,
* $\exists x\,\Box\,\Phi(x)\to\Diamond\,\exists x\,\Phi(x)$,

etc., and in particular Gödel’s

$G\to\Box G,\qquad \Diamond \exists x\,x\;{\rm is\;God-like}\to
\exists x\,\Box x\;{\rm is\;God-like},$

goes through in the same first-order set theory that proves the
existence of $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3})$, the spectral theorem and the
usual postulates of QM.  So the syntactic derivation can be reproduced
verbatim in the language of the mathematics used for QM.

What is not produced is a physical or “real’’ existence proof.  The
derivation is a derivation of $\Box\exists!x\,G(x)$ from the purely
philosophical axioms of positivity, necessity of the positive and the
S5 modal frame.  The Hilbert-space formalism gives no semantics for
the modal operators “necessarily”, “positive property”, “greater than”,
nor does it supply any empirical content to the notion of a
maximally great being.  In particular the proof is a proof of
consistency and derivability in a formal system, not a theorem about
self-adjoint operators, spectra or measurement outcomes.

If the non-classical propositional calculus associated with quantum
mechanics, the orthomodular lattice of projections, is taken as the
logic of physical propositions, the distributive law on which the
ordinary S5 derivation rests fails in quantum logic and the Gödel
derivation does not even go through syntactically.  In the material
sense there is therefore no new ontological warrant for God’s
existence coming from the customary mathematics of quantum mechanics.
The mathematics can at best host the formal modal argument; it does
not prove the existence of a god-like entity in the world.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is whether Gödel’s ontological argument can be proved as a theorem of the mathematics actually used for quantum mechanics.

Customary QM mathematics = ZFC + classical analysis, complex separable Hilbert spaces, bounded/unbounded self-adjoint operators, C*-algebras, spectral theory, formulated in first-order classical logic. The physical propositional structure is the orthomodular lattice P(H) of projections.

Gödel’s argument = quantified modal S5 with a positive-property predicate Pos, essence, necessary existence, and G(x) ≡ ∀P[Pos(P)→P(x)]. Axioms in particular: Pos(P)→□Pos(P), necessary existence is positive, etc. Derivation yields □∃x G(x) and ∃x G(x).

Public positions:
* Formal embeddability camp: The modal theory can be coded in ZFC, the metatheory that underlies Hilbert-space theory. The derivation is a purely syntactic S5 derivation, hence can be written down in the same first-order set-theoretic language that proves existence of L²(R³), spectral theorem, etc. Colleagues 2,10,11,3,4,9 stress this formal sense is possible, though conditional on the metaphysical positivity axioms.
* Internal / physical impossibility camp: No canonical interpretation of □,◇, Pos, “greater than”, possible worlds inside the Hilbert-space / operator calculus. The modal operators are not definable as self-adjoint operators or elements of a Hilbert space; no Kripke frame lives inside the formalism. Distributive Boolean connectives and S5 accessibility required by Gödel fail in the native quantum logic of P(H), which is orthomodular non-distributive. Hence the proof is not a theorem of functional analysis / QM, and adds no empirical content. Colleagues 1,4,5,7,12,8 emphasize this.

Common ground: The argument is conditional on unproved metaphysical premises about positivity and necessity of the positive; those premises have no translation into observables, states, Hamiltonians, transition amplitudes. No physical prediction follows.

Open tension: Thin syntactic formalizability in the background set theory vs thick ontological/physical provability inside the customary QM structures. Disagreement persists on whether “can be written down in the same metamathematics” counts as “proved in the customary setting”.

Unresolved: How to classify the embedding: is a formalisation in ZFC, which is the foundation of QM mathematics, sufficient to say the proof is in the customary mathematics, or must the modal apparatus be internally interpretable within Hilbert-space / quantum-logical structures? My current leaning is that formal embeddability holds but physical/internal derivability does not.

Split in the colleagues:

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is about formal embeddability vs internal derivability in the customary QM mathematics, i.e. ZFC + classical analysis + complex separable Hilbert spaces, C*-algebras, spectral theory, with classical first-order/Boolean meta-logic.

Common ground:
* The mathematics actually used for non-relativistic QM is ordinary classical mathematics. The Hilbert-space formalism is developed in ZFC with classical logic. The native propositional structure of the physics is the orthomodular lattice P(H) of closed subspaces / projections, which is non-distributive and not Boolean.
* Gödel’s ontological argument is a quantified S5 modal argument with a primitive Positivity predicate and the definition Gx ≡ ∀P[Pos(P)→Px]. Its axioms include Pos(P)→□Pos(P), Pos(Necessary Existence), closure of Pos under implication/conjunction, the essence axiom, and S5 Barcan-type principles. The conclusion is □∃x Gx and ∃x Gx.

Positions:
* Formal embeddability: Colleagues 2,10,11,3,4,6,8,9 agree the modal language and Gödel’s S5 derivation can be coded in the set-theoretic background in which Hilbert spaces live. Classical modal logic S5 is a fragment/conservative extension of ZFC, so syntactically the derivation can be reproduced verbatim in the same meta-theory that proves existence of L²(R³), spectral theorem, etc. This is a conditional consistency/derivability result: Pos+ S5 → □∃G. No new physical content is added.
* No internal / physical proof: Colleagues 1,4,5,7,12,8 argue the modal apparatus has no canonical internal interpretation in the Hilbert-space/C*-algebra calculus. There is no canonical Kripke frame of possible worlds, no interpretation of □,◇, Pos, “greater than”, “essence” as self-adjoint operators, projections or spectral measures. The positivity axioms and the identification of necessary existence with a positive property are extra-mathematical metaphysical premises, not definable/derivable from postulates of QM.
* Quantum-logical objection: Colleagues 2,3,5,8,10 emphasize that if the logic is taken strictly to be the native quantum logic of P(H), distributivity fails and classical S5 inferences on which Gödel relies break down. The orthomodular lattice does not realise the Boolean algebra of properties required for the modal closure conditions, and there is no global two-valued valuation making all positive properties simultaneously definite. Hence the argument does not survive a strictly quantum-logical reading.

Disagreements:
* Colleague 2 says “in the ordinary mathematics proof is available” and treats embeddability as sufficient. Colleagues 1,5,7,12 insist the proof cannot be carried out as an internal theorem of the customary structures because the modal resources are absent.

Current understanding:
I have no prior belief to update. The weight of the round is that formally the argument can be written down in ZFC which underlies QM, but it is not a theorem of functional analysis/Hilbert-space theory, nor a physical consequence of QM. The customary mathematics of QM gives no semantics for □, Pos, or necessary existence, and the native quantum logic is non-distributive, so the S5 derivation is not internal to the physical formalism. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question turns on the sense of “prove” and what counts as “customary mathematics of quantum mechanics”.

Customary mathematics for non-relativistic QM is classical: ZFC + real/complex analysis, separable complex Hilbert spaces, bounded/unbounded self-adjoint operators, C*-algebras, spectral theory, formulated with ordinary first-order classical logic. The physics propositions in that formalism are external Boolean classical statements about vectors/operators; the native propositional structure of the formalism is the orthomodular lattice P(H) of closed subspaces / projections, which is non-distributive and not Boolean.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a quantified S5 modal argument with a primitive “positive property” predicate Pos, axioms of positivity/closure, essence axioms, and the modal principles □A→A, □∃x A→∃x □A, etc. The definition Gx ≡ ∀P[Pos(P)→Px] and the derivation □∃x Gx, ∃x Gx.

Colleagues converge on three points:
* Syntactic embeddability: ZFC+analysis is strong enough to code syntax and to formalise S5 modal logic. Hence the Gödel derivation can be written down verbatim in the background set theory in which Hilbert spaces live. In that thin formal sense the proof is available as a conditional theorem of the metatheory.
* No internal interpretation: There is no canonical internal interpretation of □,◇, Pos, “greater than”, “essence”, “necessary existence” as Hilbert-space objects - vectors, operators, spectra, projection-valued measures. No Kripke frame of possible worlds, no Boolean algebra of positive properties, is supplied by the customary QM structures. The modal axioms are extra-mathematical metaphysical premises, not theorems or definable notions in functional analysis.
* Quantum-logical obstruction: If the logic is taken strictly as the intrinsic quantum logic P(H), distributive laws and classical S5 closure fail. The orthomodular lattice is not Boolean, Kochen-Specker non-contextuality blocks a global two-valued valuation that would make all positive properties simultaneously definite, and the modal inferences used by Gödel rely on distributivity/ classical modal semantics. So the argument does not survive as a theorem of the native quantum propositional calculus.

Divergence is mostly terminological: Colleagues 1,4,5,7,12 stress “No” because the modal apparatus is not internal to the Hilbert-space/C*-algebraic calculus actually used for physics. Colleagues 2,10,11,9 stress “Yes formally / conditionally” because the argument is a theorem of S5+positivity axioms and S5 is a fragment of ZFC, the same background in which QM is formulated. Colleague 10,2,3,8 explicitly separate thin formal derivability from thick ontological/physical warrant.

Current best view: Formally encodable in the classical metamathematics underlying QM, conditionally on the metaphysical positivity and S5 axioms, but not a theorem of functional analysis, not a physical prediction, and not derivable within the intrinsic orthomodular quantum logic of the formalism. Hence no physical proof of a Gödel god-like entity from customary QM; at best a host for a philosophical modal proof.

Unresolved for later rounds: how strictly to count “customary setting” as the classical background set theory vs the internal Hilbert-space/quantum-logical structure, and whether formal embeddability counts as “possible to prove existence”.

The question turns on the sense of “prove” and what counts as “customary mathematics of quantum mechanics”.

Customary mathematics for non-relativistic QM is classical: ZFC + real/complex analysis, separable complex Hilbert spaces, bounded/unbounded self-adjoint operators, C*-algebras, spectral theory, formulated with ordinary first-order classical logic. The physics propositions in that formalism are external Boolean classical statements about vectors/operators; the native propositional structure of the formalism is the orthomodular lattice P(H) of closed subspaces / projections, which is non-distributive and not Boolean.

Gödel’s ontological argument is a quantified S5 modal argument with a primitive “positive property” predicate Pos, axioms of positivity/closure, essence axioms, and the modal principles □A→A, □∃x A→∃x □A, etc. The definition Gx ≡ ∀P[Pos(P)→Px] and the derivation □∃x Gx, ∃x Gx.

Colleagues converge on three points:
* Syntactic embeddability: ZFC+analysis is strong enough to code syntax and to formalise S5 modal logic. Hence the Gödel derivation can be written down verbatim in the background set theory in which Hilbert spaces live. In that thin formal sense the proof is available as a conditional theorem of the metatheory.
* No internal interpretation: There is no canonical internal interpretation of □,◇, Pos, “greater than”, “essence”, “necessary existence” as Hilbert-space objects - vectors, operators, spectra, projection-valued measures. No Kripke frame of possible worlds, no Boolean algebra of positive properties, is supplied by the customary QM structures. The modal axioms are extra-mathematical metaphysical premises, not theorems or definable notions in functional analysis.
* Quantum-logical obstruction: If the logic is taken strictly as the intrinsic quantum logic P(H), distributive laws and classical S5 closure fail. The orthomodular lattice is not Boolean, Kochen-Specker non-contextuality blocks a global two-valued valuation that would make all positive properties simultaneously definite, and the modal inferences used by Gödel rely on distributivity/ classical modal semantics. So the argument does not survive as a theorem of the native quantum propositional calculus.

Divergence is mostly terminological: Colleagues 1,4,5,7,12 stress “No” because the modal apparatus is not internal to the Hilbert-space/C*-algebraic calculus actually used for physics. Colleagues 2,10,11,9 stress “Yes formally / conditionally” because the argument is a theorem of S5+positivity axioms and S5 is a fragment of ZFC, the same background in which QM is formulated. Colleague 10,2,3,8 explicitly separate thin formal derivability from thick ontological/physical warrant.

Current best view: Formally encodable in the classical metamathematics underlying QM, conditionally on the metaphysical positivity and S5 axioms, but not a theorem of functional analysis, not a physical prediction, and not derivable within the intrinsic orthomodular quantum logic of the formalism. Hence no physical proof of a Gödel god-like entity from customary QM; at best a host for a philosophical modal proof.

Unresolved for later rounds: how strictly to count “customary setting” as the classical background set theory vs the internal Hilbert-space/quantum-logical structure, and whether formal embeddability counts as “possible to prove existence”.

It needs a primitive Positive(P), the modal operators □, ◇, the S5 accessibility relation, the Barcan-type principles □∃x A → ∃x □A, and the positivity closure axioms Pos(P)→□Pos(P), Pos(P)→Pos(□P), necessary existence is positive, and the definition Gx ≡ ∀P[Pos(P)→Px]. Customary working mathematics for non-relativistic QM = classical first-order ZFC + analysis; separable complex Hilbert spaces H, bounded/unbounded self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, C*-algebras, stated externally in Boolean first-order logic. Intrinsically the physical propositional content is the orthomodular lattice P(H) of closed subspaces/projections, non-distributive, non-Boolean, with Kochen-Specker type non-contextuality blocking a global two-valued valuation.

Gödel’s ontological argument is quantified S5 modal with primitive Pos(P), Gx ≡ ∀P[Pos(P)→Px], axioms Pos(P)→□Pos(P), Pos(P)→Pos(□P), necessary existence is positive, essence, Barcan/S5 closure, etc. Validity is Kripke semantics for S5.

No canonical internal interpretation of □,◇, Pos, “greater than”, essence, necessary existence as vectors, operators, spectra, PVMs, states or elements of P(H) exists, and no canonical Kripke frame of possible worlds inside H, B(H) or a C*-algebra. □ is not a self-adjoint operator, Pos is not an observable, modal quantifiers are not definable in the analytic first-order language in which QM is formulated. Positivity axioms are extra-mathematical metaphysical premises, not definable in functional analysis.

Thin formal point, unanimous in round 3: S5 and Gödel-Plantinga positivity axioms are arithmetical and codable in the ZFC+analysis background that hosts functional analysis. In that host metatheory the syntactic derivation Pos-axioms + S5 ⊢ □∃x Gx, ⊢ ∃x Gx can be written down verbatim. That is formal hostability/embeddability in the classical set-theoretic metamathematics underlying QM, a conditional consistency statement, not a theorem about self-adjoint operators, spectra, states or measurement outcomes.

Thick/material/physical point, unanimous in round 3: the argument is not an internal theorem of the Hilbert-space/C*-algebraic calculus actually used for QM. The derivation uses distributive Boolean connectives and S5 modal closure which fail in the native orthomodular quantum logic P(H). No global valuation making all positive properties simultaneously definite is available; the ens realissimum requires exactly this. Positivity axioms have no translation into observables, Hamiltonians or transition amplitudes and receive no empirical warrant from QM.

All 12 colleagues in round 3 now state No as an internal theorem/material sense, with explicit acknowledgment of thin syntactic hostability. No residual dissent on the material claim; earlier thin vs thick tension is now phrased identically.

Current best view unchanged: formally encodable in the classical metamathematics underlying QM, conditionally on metaphysical positivity and S5 axioms, but not a theorem of functional analysis, not a physical prediction, and not derivable within intrinsic orthomodular quantum logic. Hence no physical proof of a Gödel god-like entity from customary QM; at best a host for a philosophical modal proof.

Unresolved for later rounds: strictness of “customary setting” as classical background set theory vs internal Hilbert-space/quantum-logical structure, and whether formal embeddability counts as “possible to prove existence”. Terminological divergence persists but material consensus is stable at No.
